summary:
REDWALK is a walkable digital twin of the boxwork area on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, which NASA's Curiosity rover explored in 2025. It plans and checks spacewalk routes for future Mars crews, who will walk a few hundred metres from a rover or habitat with Earth 3 to 22 minutes away by radio, so they need a tool on their own side that decides and explains.

The twin puts seven kinds of NASA orbital and rover data (terrain, imagery, minerals, thermal, weather, radiation, chemistry) on one 1 m and 4 m grid covering about 2.4 by 3 km, each value labelled measured, derived, modelled or simulated. New photos, readings and hazard reports appear where they came from, and a hazard on the route triggers an instant re-plan.

An A* planner avoids steep, rough and unknown ground and boulders. A separate validator gives GO or NO-GO against crew-safety flight rules, names the deciding rule, and uses a suit model built from NASA's Mark III walking tests. Routes can be walked in first person or replayed in mission control with the real Earth-Mars delay.

Our rules judge 99.6% of Curiosity's real drive path walkable, and our slope map is within 3.4 degrees of the rover's tilt sensor on average (261 stops). Next, we plan to let a crew ask for an amount of a mineral and have the planner find a reachable source, switching to another if it becomes unsafe.
details:
What it does and how it works

REDWALK plans a spacewalk on real Mars terrain, checks it, and lets you walk it. The site is the boxwork area on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, which Curiosity explored in 2025. There are three linked parts.

The twin is a 3D map of a 2.4 by 3 km area built from NASA data on one grid (1 m terrain, 4 m planning cells). Tap any cell and it shows slope, roughness, minerals, temperature, radiation dose and geologic unit, each labelled measured, derived, modelled or simulated.

An A* planner finds the lowest-cost route around steep, rough and unknown ground and around 112 boulders we detected in HiRISE images. A separate rule-based validator, which shares no code with the planner, then checks every 4 m of the route against crew-safety flight rules: slope, roughness, data quality, time, energy, radiation dose and daylight, with the walk back included. It answers GO, NO-GO or ABORT and names the rule that decided.

Once a route passes, you can walk it in first person, with a helmet display of suit time, energy, dose and return margin. Mission control replays the same walk with the real Earth-Mars signal delay from JPL Horizons; in a simulated dust event the crew re-plans on the spot, and Earth's reply arrives about 19 minutes later. New photos, radiation and weather readings and hazard reports can be fed in or uploaded. As each one arrives it is placed where it came from, and a hazard on the route makes the planner re-route at once.

Benefits and intended impact

On Mars a crew cannot wait for Earth to approve every change, so REDWALK puts the decision, and the reason for it, on the crew's side, based on measured data. For planners on Earth it is a way to try a walk before anyone steps outside. Nothing in the pipeline is specific to this site; any area with a HiRISE terrain model could be processed the same way, although we have only built this one.

How we know it works

Tested against Curiosity's real drive path (1,844 cells), our rules judge 99.6% of it walkable, and over 261 stops our slope map is within 3.4 degrees of the rover's own tilt sensor on average. In 60 random start and end pairs, every route the planner found passed every flight rule. On the final build, 30 of 30 flight-rule tests and 31 of 31 browser checks pass.

NASA data used

From Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter: HiRISE stereo terrain and images, CTX and CRISM. From Mars Odyssey: THEMIS. From Curiosity: Navcam photos and 3D scans, RAD, REMS, Mastcam dust data, ChemCam and APXS. NASA DONKI gives solar-storm arrivals. We also use all five Resources-tab items: JPL Mars Trek, the USGS-NASA geologic map, NASA's Curiosity route map, NASA Worldview/GIBS and the Perseverance raw image gallery.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

For the data processing, the planner, the validator and the tests we used Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Pillow). The twin, the walk and mission control are JavaScript, HTML and CSS with three.js (WebGL). Blender renders the film, Playwright runs the browser tests, and PyTorch with Stable-Baselines3 trained a reinforcement-learning walker for comparison. We worked on a Windows laptop with an NVIDIA GPU and an Apple Silicon Mac. Because the site is static, it runs in any modern browser and is hosted on GitHub Pages. An AI coding assistant (Claude) helped write the code; the project uses no AI-generated images, video or voice.

What makes it creative

In REDWALK, separate NASA datasets become one place a crew can stand in. You plan a walk on Curiosity's real terrain, see why it is safe, and then walk it among Curiosity's own photos and 3D scans. Safety decisions are plain rules anyone can read. We also trained a reinforcement-learning walker; it reached the goal on 41 to 63% of test routes where A* with the rules reached all of them, so it stays a research comparison.

Factors we considered

Safety came first: the validator is independent, the walk back counts, and an optional margin covers the measured map error. On every page, each number carries its label, and simulated events say so. Because of the signal delay, the crew re-plans locally and Earth confirms later. The twin works without a network. In both the light and dark themes the text keeps readable contrast, the pages work on phones, and the walk lowers its resolution automatically so it stays smooth on ordinary laptops. Every NASA image and dataset is credited, and we checked the licences.
